topics.title: Managing Care: Care Models, Delegation & Handoffs
topics.summary: Managing care means organizing people, time, and money so every client gets safe, coordinated care, through the right care model, wise delegation, and complete handoffs.
objectives: You can name the goals of managed care and explain HMO vs. PPO rules to a client.
You can pick the care model that fits a unit's problem and predict its weak spot.
You can use the five rights to decide what goes to an LPN or UAP.
You can choose safe actions when a unit is suddenly short-staffed.
You can respect a client's choices safely and give a complete verbal handoff.
topics.bigPicture:
Every shift is a resource puzzle. There are only so many nurses, aides, hours, and dollars. Managing care is how the nurse turns that puzzle into safe care. It means deciding who does what, in what order, and with what information.

When a lab is drawn twice, or an aide does not know a client is newly unsteady, managing care has failed. The NCLEX tests this all the time, often without saying "managed care." Questions on delegation, assignment, priorities, handoffs, and unsafe client requests all live here. Ask one question: which choice keeps the client safest and keeps the RN doing RN-only work?
recap: The RN delegates tasks, never judgment. Assessment, planning, teaching, evaluation, and unstable clients stay with the RN.
The delegating RN stays accountable for the decision, the supervision, and the outcome.
Five rights: task, circumstance, person, directions and communication, supervision and evaluation.
"Stable with a predictable outcome" unlocks LPN assignment and UAP delegation.
HMO: gatekeeper and referrals, lower cost. PPO: self-referral, bigger network, pays more out of network.
Case method is one shift. Primary nursing is the whole stay. Functional splits by task. Team nursing is RN-led.
Nurse numbers and education affect complications, death, and cost. Match skill mix to acuity.
Respect choices but never join unsafe care. Hand off with documentation plus a verbal report.

keyTerms.def: A system that coordinates care and resources for enrolled clients, to lower cost, cut waste, and improve outcomes.
A plan with a restricted network. The primary care provider is the gatekeeper, who tracks care and must refer to specialists. Lower cost in network.
A plan with a larger network and no gatekeeper. Clients may self-refer. Out-of-network care is allowed but costs more.
Care that puts the client and family at the center of decisions and respects their values, while still doing no harm.
Sorting roles (UAP, LPN, RN, NP) by education and skill so each person works at the top of their license.
Bedside nurses and leaders share decisions about practice and resources, often through unit councils.
One nurse gives all care to assigned clients for one shift. Common in ICU and ED.
Work is split by task, such as one nurse giving all medications. Efficient, but care becomes fragmented.
An RN team leader directs LPNs and UAP for a group of clients.
One RN plans and is accountable for care for the whole stay. Others follow the plan when that RN is off.
Licensed practical or vocational nurse. Cares for stable clients under RN or provider direction. No initial or full assessment.
Unlicensed assistive personnel, such as aides and CNAs. They do delegated basic care that needs no nursing judgment.
Giving a competent person a selected nursing task for a selected client. The RN stays accountable.
Giving work a person is already allowed to do in their own scope, like a stable client to an LPN.
How sick a client is and how much nursing care is needed.
The share of RNs, LPNs, and UAP on a unit. It should match acuity.
The ethical duty to do no harm.
Passing information and responsibility for a client to another caregiver, shift, or facility.

sections.heading: What is managed care?
sections.keyIdea: Managed care plans care from first contact to the end of a health problem, to cut cost and waste and improve outcomes.
sections.body:
Managed care coordinates care and resources for a group of enrolled clients. It grew because costs kept rising. Payers (insurers and government) wanted to stop paying for repeated or unneeded care. So care is planned from the first contact until the problem is solved.

Some payer trends help, like more preventive care. Some add risk, like earlier discharge, which can raise readmissions if teaching is rushed.

Your course names three nurse functions. Delegation frees the RN for RN-only work. Care coordination and time management orders care so nothing is repeated. Interpersonal skills are called the heart of managed care.

Two plan types show up on the exam. An HMO trades choice for lower cost. A PPO trades higher cost for more choice.
bullets: Lower costs and eliminate redundancy (repeat tests).
Promote consistency (same protocols for all).
Increase efficiency.
Improve outcomes.
Enhance client satisfaction.
sections.example: A client with Parkinson disease tires quickly. PT and a swallowing test are both set for 1000. The nurse moves the swallow test to 1400, after a rest. That one call is care coordination.

check.q: A client in an HMO books an orthopedic surgeon found online. What should the nurse clarify?
check.a: Whether the client has a referral from the primary care provider (the gatekeeper) and whether the surgeon is in network. Without these, the visit may not be covered.

sections.heading: Who does what: RN, LPN, or UAP?
sections.keyIdea: If a task needs judgment, or the client is new or unstable, it stays with the RN.
sections.body:
The RN does the first and ongoing full assessment. The RN makes the care plan, teaches, evaluates, and cares for unstable clients.

The LPN/LVN cares for stable clients with predictable outcomes, under RN or provider direction. The LPN collects data and reinforces teaching the RN already did. UAP do basic care that needs no judgment.

Watch out: a simple task can still be off-limits. Feeding is a UAP task. But a client who newly coughs with liquids needs RN assessment first. Food or fluid may be going into the lungs (aspiration).

rows: Assessment, care plan, teaching, evaluation, unstable clients, delegation
Stable clients, routine treatments, dressing changes, many medications, data collection
Initial assessment, care plan, first teaching, unstable clients
Hygiene, feeding help, walking, toileting, linens, intake and output, routine vital signs and specimens on stable clients
Assessment, teaching, medications, interpreting findings, unstable clients

check.q: A UAP must feed two clients. One has dementia and eats well with cues. One had a stroke yesterday and has no swallow screen yet. Which may the UAP feed?
check.a: The client with dementia, who is stable. The stroke client may aspirate and stays NPO until the swallow screen is done.

sections.heading: Seven ways to organize nursing care
sections.keyIdea: Find the model by asking who owns the client's care, and for how long.
sections.body:
A care delivery model answers one question: how do we divide the work? Look for two clues: who owns the client's care, and for how long. "All care, this shift" is case method. "All care, the whole stay" is primary nursing.

Exam items rarely ask for a definition. They describe a unit with a problem. Work backward from the problem to the model that fixes it.
bullets: Care split up, emotional needs missed: the functional method; switch to team or primary.
Basic care missed, nobody owns it: team nursing.
Very unstable clients: case method (ICU, ED).
Poor continuity over a long stay: primary nursing.
Nurses feel unheard, high turnover: shared governance.
RNs doing linens while assessments run late: differentiated practice.

rows: Client and family at the center
Must balance requests with no harm
Roles set by education and skill
One nurse, all care, one shift
One RN owns the plan for the stay
Needs many RNs and good handoffs

sections.analogy: The functional method is like a restaurant assembly line: fast, but nobody knows if the diner is happy.
sections.example: A nursing facility has missed trays, linens, and baths, though staffing is adequate. Team nursing fixes it. RN leaders assign named residents to named aides and check completion.

check.q: One nurse gives all medications, one takes all vital signs, one does all treatments. Clients say nobody explains anything. Which model is this?
check.a: The functional method. It is efficient and cheap, but no one knows the whole client, so care is fragmented and teaching and emotional needs are missed.

sections.heading: Delegation vs. assignment: what's the difference?
sections.keyIdea: The RN can hand off tasks, never judgment, and stays accountable for the result.
sections.body:
Delegation means giving a competent person one nursing task for one client. The RN stays accountable. The RN answers for the choice to delegate, the supervision, and the outcome. The other person is responsible for doing the task correctly.

Assignment gives work already inside the person's own scope, like a stable client to an LPN.

Never delegate assessment, care planning, teaching, evaluation, or unstable clients. Use the five rights below, from the national NCSBN–ANA guidelines. If any right fails, do not delegate.
steps: Right task: routine and free of judgment? Walking a stable client: yes. Teaching insulin: no.
Right circumstance: is this client stable with a predictable outcome today?
Right person: is this person trained and skilled in the task?
Right directions: say what to do, by when, and what to report right away. "Tell me if the systolic pressure is above 160."
Right supervision and evaluation: follow up, check the client yourself, and give feedback.

check.q: A UAP reports a pulse of 118 on a stable post-op client. Who interprets it?
check.a: The RN. The UAP collected and reported data. Interpreting it and acting is nursing judgment, which cannot be delegated.

sections.heading: What if the unit is short-staffed?
sections.keyIdea: Protect RN-only work, delegate only routine tasks, and escalate for help.
sections.body:
Both the number of nurses and their education affect morbidity (complications), mortality (death), and cost. Too many clients per nurse means more errors, falls, and missed assessments.

Staffing is measured by nurse-to-patient ratio or nursing hours per patient day. Most states use staffing committees or rules to publicly report staffing. Few set fixed ratios by law. Retirements, rising specialty demand, and pandemic burnout add stress.

So skill mix must match acuity. When a unit suddenly loses nurses, "work faster" is not the answer. Do this:
bullets: Escalate through the chain of command for more staff.
Give RNs unstable clients, admissions, and assessments.
Give stable, routine clients to the LPN.
Delegate routine tasks to UAP with clear report rules.
Cluster care, and use critical pathways to protect key safety steps.
Never push RN-only work onto UAP.
sections.example: Three nurses call out at 0700. The charge nurse calls the supervisor first. RNs take fresh post-op clients and a heparin drip. The LPN takes stable clients on oral medications. UAP do hygiene and routine vital signs.

check.q: A manager suggests UAP do admission assessments "just for today." What should the charge nurse do?
check.a: Decline and escalate. Initial assessment is RN work no matter the staffing.

sections.heading: Two safety alerts: client choices and handoffs
sections.keyIdea: Honor choices without joining unsafe care, and never rely on paperwork alone at a handoff.
sections.body:
Safety alert 1. Patient-focused care does not mean doing whatever the client asks. The nurse also must do no harm (nonmaleficence). Explain the risk calmly and without judgment. Ask why, and offer a safe option that meets the real wish. A competent adult may refuse care after an informed talk, but the nurse never takes part in unsafe care.

Safety alert 2. Information gets lost at transfers and shift changes. Document fully AND give a verbal report whenever possible. A written packet alone is not enough. SBAR keeps the report complete.

Related concepts, listed below, often decide close calls between two answers.
steps: Situation: who the client is and what is happening now.
Background: history, allergies, code status, medications and last doses.
Assessment: vital signs, pain, mobility, skin, lines, recent changes.
Recommendation: what to do and watch next.
Read-back: invite questions; confirm key items.
sections.example: A dizzy client asks to turn off the bed alarm because it is "humiliating." The nurse says, "I worry you could fall. Let's check on you hourly and keep the alarm on its quietest setting." Dignity is honored, and safety stays.

check.q: A competent client with heart failure removes the nasal cannula because it hurts the ears. SpO2 is 90%. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Ask why, explain the risk, and offer fixes like ear padding, or ask the provider about another device. If the client still declines, respect it, notify the provider, and document the talk. Do not force the oxygen, and do not just leave it off without discussing the risk.

bullets: Advocacy: speak up for fair access to care.
Clinical decision making: set priorities; avoid repeat tests.
Communication: keep the team and family informed.
Ethics: autonomy, dignity, justice, and do no harm.
Healthcare systems: follow the rules while controlling cost.
Teaching and learning: prevent complications; mentor newer staff.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Most wrong answers come from mixing up two terms that sound alike; learn the one clue that separates them.
sections.body: These pairs cause most missed questions in this topic. Read the clue column, then look for that clue in the stem.

rows: One shift vs. the whole stay
RN leads whole-client care vs. one task for everyone
Sorting roles by credentials vs. sharing decision power
Handing off a task vs. work already in the person's scope
Needs a referral vs. can self-refer but pays more
Informed choice does not mean the nurse helps cause harm
UAP and LPN report data; the RN interprets

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Cross out assessment and teaching verbs, then cross out new or unstable clients.
sections.body: Watch the verbs. "Assess," "teach," "evaluate," and "determine" mean RN work. "Assist," "obtain," "measure," and "ambulate" mean a UAP may do it for a stable client.
bullets: Delegation: which task fits a UAP?
Assignment: which client fits the LPN?
Model fit: which model fixes this unit's problem?
Leadership: short staffing, unsafe requests, or handoffs.
steps: Read the stem: Which task can go to the UAP? (A) Teach a new incentive spirometer. (B) Get a clean-catch urine from a stable client. (C) Determine whether a foot wound is healing. (D) Feed a client who began coughing at breakfast.
What is it really asking? Which task is routine, for a stable client, with no judgment?
Key cues: "new," "determine," and "began coughing."
Why the others are wrong: (A) is first teaching. (C) is assessment. (D) suggests aspiration risk.
The answer is (B). A routine specimen is a UAP task.
Reusable strategy: cross out assessment and teaching verbs, then new or unstable clients.

sections.heading: Worked case: the team leader's morning
sections.keyIdea: Keep new, unstable, and teaching clients; give stable care to others with clear report rules.
sections.body: You are the RN team leader with one LPN and one UAP. Here are your six clients. Build a safe assignment.
bullets: 1: new pneumonia admission, SpO2 91% on 2 L.
2: stable diabetes, discharge tomorrow, needs new insulin pen teaching.
3: day 3 after bowel surgery, stable, needs a dressing change and oral medications.
4: dementia, full help with bathing and feeding, swallows safely.
5: first unit of red blood cells starts at 0800.
6: stable heart failure, needs daily weight and intake and output.
steps: Notice cues: Client 1 is new and low on oxygen. Client 5 is starting blood, and the first 15 minutes carry the most risk. Client 2 needs new teaching. Clients 3, 4, and 6 are stable.
Prioritize: assess Client 1 first. Be at Client 5's bedside when the blood starts.
Assign the LPN: Clients 3 and 6.

Delegate to the UAP: care for Client 4, plus Client 6's weight and intake and output. "Weigh before breakfast on the same scale. Tell me right away if the weight is up more than 1 kg from yesterday or the client is short of breath."
Keep for yourself: Clients 1, 2, and 5, plus supervising everyone.
Evaluate: check in mid-morning and reassess anyone outside your limits.

check.q: At 0930 the UAP says Client 4 coughs and has a wet voice after sips of water. What should the RN do?
check.a: Stop oral intake and assess for aspiration personally. The client is no longer stable, so feeding cannot be delegated until the plan is updated.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: North Carolina rules match this lesson: the RN delegates tasks, not judgment.
sections.body: The North Carolina Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the NC Nursing Practice Act. Its rules match this lesson.
bullets: Law: G.S. 90-171.19 et seq. (Chapter 90, Article 9A). Rules: 21 NCAC 36 .0224 (RN) and .0225 (LPN).
The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. The LPN works under RN or provider supervision.
Nurse Aide I registry: NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation. Nurse Aide II registry: NCBON; must also be on the NA I registry.
NA II tasks include some sterile or advanced tasks, such as sterile dressing changes and oxygen.
The task must be on the aide's list AND right for this client now.
NCBON publishes a Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP and a scope-of-practice decision tree.
Practice events go through NCBON's Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool: human error, at-risk, or reckless behavior.
Conduct issues (diversion, impairment, fraud, boundary or confidentiality breaches) are reported to the Board.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state. The nurse follows the practice laws of the state where the client is located.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 39 study guide, pp. 2621–2625: managed care, HMO vs. PPO (p. 2622), care models (pp. 2622–2624), Safety Alerts (p. 2623), staffing evidence (p. 2624), related concepts (p. 2625). Scenarios: staff loss (p. 2624) and SNF care (p. 2626).
bullets: The source says only California mandates hospital ratios. Oregon has since passed statewide hospital ratios (2023 law, phased in from 2024); Massachusetts mandates ICU ratios.
Most states still use staffing committees or disclosure.
Added the five rights and delegation vs. assignment (NCSBN–ANA guidelines).
Added SBAR for the Safety Alert on verbal handoffs.
Added that HMOs generally cover emergencies out of network.
"Client" replaces "patient."

mnemonics.name: Keep the "TAPE-U" with the RN
mnemonics.text: Teaching, Assessment, Planning, Evaluation, Unstable clients: never delegated to UAP.

mnemonics.name: Shift vs. stay
mnemonics.text: Case method = this Shift. Primary nursing = the whole Stay. Functional = one Function for everybody. Team = an RN leads a Team.

pearls: The delegating RN stays accountable for the decision, supervision, and outcome.
Any new or changing finding sends the client back to the RN.
UAP collect data; only the RN interprets it.
In a staffing crisis, escalate and protect RN-only work.
A written transfer form alone is an incomplete handoff.
redFlags: A client becomes unstable during a delegated task: assess now and stop delegating.
Being told to delegate assessment or teaching "because we are short": refuse and escalate.
A handoff with no verbal report.
A request to remove a safety measure without a talk about risks.
A high-acuity unit staffed mostly by unlicensed staff: risk of missed assessments, falls, and failure to rescue.

checks.q: The RN leads an LPN and a UAP. Clients: a chest-pain admission from 20 minutes ago, a stable day-2 appendectomy, and a client who needs shower help. Who gets whom?
checks.a: The RN takes the new chest-pain client. The LPN takes the stable post-op client. The UAP helps with the shower, with clear report rules.

checks.q: Nurses say they have no voice in unit policies, and turnover is high. Which model helps?
checks.a: Shared governance, such as a staff council that votes on a new fall protocol.

checks.q: A primary nurse in the ICU is off for two days. What happens to the client's plan?
checks.a: Associate nurses follow it. The plan is not put on hold, and a clear handoff keeps continuity.

checks.q: A UAP reports a blood pressure of 88/50, down from 124/76, and offers to recheck in an hour. What should the RN do?
checks.a: Assess the client now. A big change needs RN assessment and maybe provider notification.

topics.title: Case Management & Critical Pathways
topics.summary: Case management coordinates health and social services over time for clients with complex or chronic needs, using critical pathways and revising the plan whenever things change.
objectives: You can pick which client needs a case manager most.
You can list the case manager's four core responsibilities in order.
You can name the four parts of a critical pathway and the five elements of a strong program.
You can respond correctly to a pathway variance as a bedside nurse.
You can recognize when a discharge plan must be revised.
You can match case management services to vulnerable groups across the lifespan.
topics.bigPicture:
Picture a client going home after brain-tumor surgery with chemotherapy. Surgery, oncology, the infusion team, the dietitian, social work, and home nursing each hold a piece of the plan. If nobody connects the pieces, an infusion is missed or a scan is done twice. Case management connects them. It coordinates care over time so a complex client moves safely from one setting to the next.

About 89% of case managers are RNs. Even at the bedside, you are part of this system. You report variances, share discharge information, and notice when a client's function slips. The NCLEX asks who needs a case manager, what to do when a client falls off the pathway, and when the plan must change.
recap: Case management coordinates health and social services over time for one client with complex, chronic needs.
Chronic, recurring, multi-service problems benefit most. A short, self-limited illness rarely needs it.
Four jobs in order: holistic assessment, culturally aligned planning, team coordination, and monitoring with revision.
A change in clinical condition or in discharge plans means revise the plan now.
Pathway parts: diagnosis, interventions, time frames, and expected outcomes.
For a variance, the bedside nurse assesses, keeps the client safe, and notifies per the pathway.
The case manager should be involved from admission, not on the day of discharge.
Group variance trends point to system problems that need quality review.

keyTerms.def: Coordinating a client's care over time with health and social services, across disciplines. Most helpful for multiple or complex chronic problems.
Usually an RN with a BS or MS in a health or human services field, plus supervised experience for certification.
A model where the primary care office is the client's home base for preventive, acute, and chronic care, with a personal plan.
A hospital-based case manager who coordinates care before and after discharge.
A standard, evidence-based team plan for clients with a similar, predictable condition. Also called a care map or clinical pathway.
Any time a client's progress strays from the pathway's expected timeline or outcome, such as delirium or not walking on schedule.
Standard groupings of diagnoses tied to payment. They help spot high-risk, high-cost clients.
Signs that a client needs case management, such as many comorbidities, stays of 3 days or more, or functional decline.
Another health problem a client has at the same time as the main one.
Taking many medications, often from several prescribers, which raises the risk of duplicates and harmful combinations.
A move between settings, such as hospital to home or rehab. Information is often lost here.

sections.heading: What is case management, and who needs it?
sections.keyIdea: Case management helps most when a problem is chronic, involves many services, or keeps bringing the client back.
sections.body:
Case management is coordination over time. It joins health services (nursing, medicine, therapy, pharmacy) with social services (transportation, money help, caregiver support). Its goals are a better care experience, lower cost, more choices for the client, and better population health.

It helps most with multiple or complex chronic problems, like COPD plus a hip replacement. It adds little for a short illness that resolves with standard treatment. Ask three questions: Is it chronic or recurring? Does it need several services? Is the client at risk for readmission or decline?

Case managers work in several settings, shown in the table.

rows: Primary care office is the home base for all ongoing care
Care before and after discharge for acute or complex conditions
Ongoing care at home or by phone; cost control

sections.example: Two clients share a unit. One is 34 with pneumonia, going home in 2 days. The other is 61, on home oxygen and 11 medications, living alone, on a third admission this year. Refer the second client first.

check.q: Who needs case management most: a sprained ankle, cellulitis on day 2 of antibiotics, or heart failure with two admissions in 3 months, living alone?
check.a: The client with heart failure: chronic, recurring, living alone, and needing medications, monitoring, teaching, and home services.

sections.heading: The case manager's four core jobs
sections.keyIdea: Assess first, then plan with the client, coordinate the team, and keep monitoring and revising.
sections.body: The case manager's work follows the nursing process, stretched over time and settings. Learn the four jobs in order. Exam options often test the missing or out-of-order step.
steps: Holistic (whole-person) assessment: strengths, needs, home life, caregivers, independence, and equipment such as oxygen or a walker. Assess before any referral.
Plan with cultural alignment: find barriers such as religious beliefs, cultural practices, and complementary therapies. Build a pathway-based plan with the client and family.
Coordinate the team: start consults and referrals, get orders, and share updates.
Monitor and revise: track progress toward goals set together with the client. A change in clinical condition or in discharge plans means revise right away.
sections.example: A client with a brain tumor will get chemotherapy into the spinal fluid (intrathecal) and by IV after discharge. Before discharge, the nurse confirms the nutrition screen, the social work consult, and the home health referral. The nurse also checks that infusion, oncology, and neurology visits do not conflict.

check.q: A new case manager orders a hospital bed and oxygen before meeting a client with COPD. What was skipped?
check.a: Holistic assessment. The client may already own oxygen, have no room for a bed, or have barriers that change the plan. Referrals come after assessment.

sections.heading: What makes a program work?
sections.keyIdea: High-risk triggers pick the clients, and five elements, starting with a case manager from admission, make the program succeed.
sections.body:
Managed care groups clients by DRGs, diagnosis groups tied to payment. This helps spot clients likely to be costly or to have complications. The triggers are listed below.

A program also needs five elements, shown in the table. Note the first one: the case manager starts at admission. Planning that starts on discharge day causes delays and unsafe transitions.
bullets: High-volume or high-risk diagnoses, such as hip replacement or brain injury.
Multiple comorbidities, or an acute stay of 3 days or more.
Need for a ventilator or home health care.
Functional decline during the stay.

rows: Needs are found early, not on the last day
Administration, medical staff, and support staff all take part
A shared map for predictable conditions

sections.analogy: It is like air-traffic control: the controller must be in the tower before takeoff, not at landing.

check.q: Case managers first meet clients on the morning of discharge. What is missing, and what happens?
check.a: A case manager involved from admission. Equipment, home health, and placement needs are found too late, causing delays and unsafe discharges.

sections.heading: What is a critical pathway?
sections.keyIdea: A critical pathway shows what "on track" looks like each day, so the team spots problems early.
sections.body:
A critical pathway is a standard, evidence-based team plan for a predictable condition, like a knee replacement. It has the four parts listed below.

Expected outcomes are the benchmark. Comparing what the client did with what was expected is how the team spots a variance early. Pathways also promote consistency and cut cost. They are not rigid orders. The case manager adjusts them for comorbidities like COPD or dementia.
bullets: Diagnosis (medical diagnosis or diagnoses).
Interventions across disciplines (nursing, medications, PT/OT, nutrition).
Time frames (days, hours, minutes, or visits).
Expected client outcomes for each time frame.

rows: Pain control, VTE prevention, incentive spirometry, dangle with PT
Pain at goal; circulation and sensation intact
PT twice, OT for ADLs, oral pain medicine, start discharge teaching
Stair training, home exercise plan, confirm equipment and follow-up
Meets mobility goals; ready for discharge

check.q: A draft hip pathway lists only tasks for each day. What must be added before use?
check.a: The expected client outcome for each time frame. Without it, nurses cannot tell if the client is on track.

sections.heading: When a client falls off the pathway
sections.keyIdea: The bedside nurse assesses, keeps the client safe, and notifies per the pathway; the case manager adjusts the plan and studies trends.
sections.body:
A variance can come from the client (a new complication), the system (no PT on weekends), or a provider (a late order). Your job depends on your role.

The bedside nurse spots the variance and keeps the client safe. The nurse follows the pathway's notification steps and starts the prescribed next steps. Do not ignore it, wait, or rewrite the pathway alone. If there is a cause you can treat at the bedside, such as pain, treat it first.

The case manager documents variances, adjusts the client's pathway, and studies group trends. If many clients wake slowly from anesthesia, the protocol gets reviewed. That feeds the quality system.

rows: Assess why (pain, dizziness, low BP), keep safe, notify per pathway
Document, add PT, review discharge date
Assess mental status, vital signs, and SpO2; keep safe; notify provider
Adjust pathway; consider a new discharge destination
7 of 20 clients woke slowly from anesthesia
Analyze the trend; refer the protocol for review

check.q: On day 2 of a hip pathway, the client gets lightheaded after 10 feet. What should the bedside nurse do?
check.a: Sit the client down safely and assess (orthostatic vital signs, pain). Then notify per the pathway, start the next steps, and document the variance.

sections.heading: Case management across the lifespan
sections.keyIdea: Each vulnerable group needs specific services, and safety, such as abuse or neglect, always comes first.
sections.body:
Vulnerable groups gain the most from a coordinator who links them to services and speaks up for them. The table shows the key services for each group.

Safety comes first. If a pregnant client has bruises and a partner who answers for her, speak with her alone and assess for abuse. If a dependent child is found neglected, report it to the county DSS (child protective services) right away. Do not wait for proof.

Goals must be realistic and include the client. For end of life, honor wishes such as dying at home, and raise hospice early.

rows: Chronic illness, substance use, mental illness, extreme poverty, abuse
Early prenatal care; community and government services; teaching on nutrition, mood disorders, avoiding substances, breastfeeding, preventing disease spread at birth
Children, correctable conditions (cleft lip, many heart defects)
Prematurity, congenital disease, birth injury, illness or injury
Coordinate surgeries, therapy, counseling, and home nursing until goals are met
School accommodations and long-term supports throughout childhood
Behavioral, intellectual, or mental health disability
Barriers to school, work, independent living, and ADLs
Realistic goals; counseling, vocational training, sheltered workshops, transportation, group homes, home aides, assistive technology, medication support
Older adults and end of life
Many chronic illnesses, polypharmacy, decline, terminal illness
Prevent duplicate and counteracting therapies; hospice, palliative care, advance directives, power of attorney, legal and money planning; support dying at home if desired

sections.example: A newborn has a heart defect needing staged surgeries. The case manager coordinates each stage and home nursing between them. The case manager does not stop after the first surgery. Families are linked early to financial aid and Medicaid waiver programs.

check.q: A 28-year-old with a moderate intellectual disability lives with an aging parent and wants to work. What should the plan include?
check.a: Vocational or supported employment, transportation, and future housing options planned with the client and parent. Avoid unrealistic goals and avoid deciding for the client.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Two options may both sound like coordination; the clue in the stem tells you which one fits.
sections.body: Use these distinctions when two answers sound alike.

rows: Coordination for one client vs. a payment system for a population
Critical pathway vs. individual care plan
Standard plan for a group, then adjusted vs. built for one client
Bedside vs. case manager variance action
Notify and start next steps vs. adjust the plan and study trends
Asthma with repeat ED visits vs. simple pneumonia
Ongoing clinic home base vs. hospital stay and transition
Coordinate surgery and rehab vs. long-term school and support
Caregiver can't help anymore vs. PT reports progress as planned

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: For any variance, look for a cause you can assess and treat at the bedside before escalating.
sections.body: Expect these question patterns:
bullets: Which client benefits most? Pick chronic, complex, and recurring.
A client is off the pathway. Assess, keep safe, and notify per the pathway.
Which finding needs a plan revision? A change in condition or discharge plans.
Which service fits this vulnerable client? Watch for hidden safety risks.
steps: Read the stem: Day 1 after knee replacement, the pathway expects walking. Vital signs are stable, but pain is 8/10 and the client refuses to get up. What first? (A) Document and retry tomorrow. (B) Assess the pain, give the prescribed analgesic, and retry; notify if still unmet. (C) Ask the case manager to change the discharge date. (D) Say refusing will delay discharge.
What is it really asking? The first action for a variance with a treatable cause.
Key cues: stable vital signs; pain 8/10 is the barrier.
Why the others are wrong: (A) ignores the cause. (C) changes the plan before treating the problem. (D) is coercive.
The answer is (B). Treat the cause, retry, and follow the pathway.
Reusable strategy: ask, "Can I fix the cause at the bedside right now?" before escalating.

sections.heading: Worked case: the third admission this year
sections.keyIdea: Find the practical barriers behind readmissions, plan with the client, and revise when the plan changes.
sections.body: Mrs. Alvarez, 74, has heart failure and COPD. This is her third admission in 10 months. Her husband has early dementia, and they live up one flight of stairs. She takes 12 medications from three providers. She skips her diuretic because she "can't get to the bathroom fast enough on the bus." She speaks Spanish and wants her daughter in decisions. Discharge is in 3 days.
steps: Notice cues: chronic disease, repeat admissions, polypharmacy, a specific reason for skipping, a limited caregiver, stairs, and language needs.
Assess holistically: stairs, equipment, her husband's safety, money, and how she likes to get information. Use an interpreter and include her daughter with permission.
Plan with her: medication review with pharmacy; ask the provider about diuretic timing; home health and weight monitoring; rehab; transportation help; caregiver support.

Coordinate now: referrals placed today, a follow-up visit within 7 days, and a written plan in Spanish. Add an early-warning plan: call if weight rises 1 kg in a day or 2 kg in a week, or breathing gets worse.

Revise: on day 2 her daughter can no longer stay with them. That is a change in discharge plans, so the case manager reassesses and revises the plan, such as more home health visits or short-term rehab.

check.q: Mrs. Alvarez says, "I just want to keep living at home with my husband." What is the best response?
check.a: "That is an important goal. Let's work on supports that could make it safe, like home health visits and transportation help."

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In North Carolina, any person who suspects child maltreatment or a disabled adult needing protection must report to county DSS.
sections.body: Case managers often find safety and legal issues during assessment. North Carolina rules include:
bullets: Children: NC is a universal reporting state. Under G.S. 7B-301, anyone who suspects a juvenile (under 18) is abused, neglected, or dependent, or died from maltreatment, must report to the county DSS director.
Report suspicion; do not investigate or wait for proof. Knowingly failing to report is a crime.
A suspected sexual offense against a juvenile must also be reported to law enforcement (G.S. 14-318.6). Follow agency policy.
Disabled adults: under G.S. 108A-102, anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to the county DSS director, orally or in writing.
Good-faith reporters are immune in both cases.

Minors: under G.S. 90-21.5, a minor may consent to pregnancy care (not sterilization or abortion), STI care, substance use care, and emotional care. So a pregnant 16-year-old can start prenatal care on her own consent. Age of majority is 18; emancipated minors may consent.

Advance directives: Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3) and the Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (G.S. 90-321). The MOST form travels with the client across settings.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state; phone case managers follow the laws of the state where the client is. RN assessment, planning, and evaluation are not delegated (21 NCAC 36 .0224).

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 39 study guide, Exemplar 39.A, pp. 2626–2629: roles and settings, core jobs, triggers and five elements (p. 2627), pathways and variances (pp. 2626, 2628), lifespan (pp. 2628–2629). PCMH from p. 2626.
bullets: The source mentions lifetime insurance caps. Under the ACA, most plans can no longer set lifetime dollar limits on essential benefits. Early financial referral is still correct.
The client, system, and provider variance types and the sample knee pathway are added as examples.
Heart failure thresholds (1 kg in a day, 2 kg in a week) are common teaching; prescribers may differ.
"Client" replaces the source's "patient."

mnemonics.name: Four jobs: "A Plan Comes Monitored"
mnemonics.text: Assess, Plan, Coordinate, Monitor and revise.

pearls: Pick the chronic, complex, recurring client for case management.
The case manager starts at admission, not discharge day.
A caregiver who backs out is a change in discharge plans: revise.
Same variance in many clients means a system problem.
redFlags: Function declines during the stay, such as now needing two people to transfer.
A caregiver suddenly can't help, or the home is unsafe.
A pregnant client with bruises and a controlling partner.
A dependent child or adult who appears neglected.
Polypharmacy from several prescribers with duplicate or clashing drugs: reconcile before discharge.

checks.q: A client with Parkinson disease walked with a cane on admission. On day 4 the client needs two people to transfer. Discharge home tomorrow is planned. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Treat it as a red flag. Reassess function, report the decline to the case manager and provider, involve PT/OT and the family, and revise the discharge plan (home health vs. rehab) before discharge.

checks.q: Most colectomy clients miss the day-2 walking goal only on weekends. What does this suggest?
checks.a: A system variance, like low weekend PT staffing. Analyze the trend and refer it for quality review.

checks.q: A client with cancer says, "I don't want to die in the hospital." What is the best response?
checks.a: "Let's talk about what you would need at home, including whether hospice could help."

checks.q: A clinic becomes a patient-centered medical home. What does it mean for the client?
checks.a: The office becomes the home base that coordinates all ongoing care.

checks.q: A case manager finds a child with cerebral palsy thin, in a soiled bed, with a new pressure injury. What first?
checks.a: Make sure the child's urgent medical needs are met and report suspected neglect to the county DSS (child protective services) right away. Do not wait for more proof.

topics.title: Cost-Effective Care, Insurance & Health Systems
topics.summary: Cost-effective care gets the best outcome for the resources used; nurses help by preventing complications and readmissions, cutting waste, explaining coverage, and advocating, never by trading away safety.
objectives: You can explain why U.S. costs are high while outcomes lag.
You can tell public insurance, private insurance, and out-of-pocket payment apart, and compare Medicare with Medicaid.
You can use premium, deductible, co-pay, and coinsurance to explain a client's bill.
You can explain how DRGs and prospective payment reward preventing complications and readmissions.
You can compare the four international health-system types.
You can choose nursing actions that save money and keep clients safe.
topics.bigPicture:
Health care costs are not just a manager's problem. A client gets a catheter infection, falls and breaks a hip, or comes back in 5 days because nobody checked that the inhaler was affordable. The cost is human first and money second. Cost-effective care means the best outcome for the money and effort spent.

Almost every cost-saving nursing action is also a safety action. Prevent complications, avoid repeat tests, teach well, and link clients to help they can use. On the NCLEX, cost questions hide inside teaching, advocacy, and safety items. One rule wins nearly every time: saving money never justifies risking safety, scope, or the standard of care.
recap: The U.S. spends the most of any high-income country but has worse outcomes, including the lowest life expectancy.
Payment comes from public insurance, private insurance, or out-of-pocket money.
Medicare: federal, age 65+ or qualifying disability, not income-based. Medicaid: federal–state, income-based, covers long-term custodial care.
Premium keeps coverage. Deductible is paid first. Co-pay is a fixed fee. Coinsurance is a percentage after the deductible.
Under PPS, payment is set in advance by DRG, so complications and extra days cost the hospital.
Four systems: socialized medicine, socialized insurance, mandatory insurance, voluntary insurance.
For a cost barrier: assess, tell the prescriber, refer. Never advise skipping or cutting medication.
Cost savings never justify compromising safety, scope, or the standard of care.

keyTerms.def: The best outcome for the resources used, by preventing complications and cutting waste, without lowering safety or quality.
Government-funded coverage for people who meet eligibility rules, such as Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP.
Coverage from companies such as Blue Cross Blue Shield, Kaiser Permanente, or Aetna, through an employer or bought individually.
Money the client pays directly, either as self-pay or as cost sharing in a plan.
Federal insurance for people 65 and older and some younger people with qualifying disabilities, end-stage renal disease, or ALS. Parts: A hospital, B outpatient, C Medicare Advantage, D drugs.
Joint federal–state insurance for eligible people with low income. Rules vary by state. A major payer for long-term nursing-home care.
The regular payment that keeps insurance active, whether or not care is used.
The yearly amount the client pays before the plan starts paying.
A fixed fee for a service or prescription, such as $30 per office visit.
The client's percentage share of a covered cost after the deductible, such as 20%.
Standard groupings of diagnoses and procedures used to set a fixed payment for a hospital stay.
The payer sets payment in advance by DRG. If care costs less, the hospital keeps the difference; if more, it absorbs the loss.
Disability-adjusted life years: a measure of disease burden that combines years lost to early death and years lived with disability.
Care and monitoring at a distance using technology. It saves cost and improves access, especially for rural and chronically ill clients.

sections.heading: How does the U.S. compare with other countries?
sections.keyIdea: The U.S. spends the most, yet its outcomes lag other high-income countries, so spending more does not equal better health.
sections.body:
The Commonwealth Fund compares the U.S. with other high-income countries. The U.S. spends the most on health care. Yet it has the highest obesity rate, chronic disease burden, and suicide rate, and the lowest life expectancy. In 2017 its DALY rate was 31% higher than in other developed countries.

Why so costly? The main drivers are administrative waste, high drug prices, and public health shocks. COVID-19 was estimated to cost more than $16 trillion. Proposed fixes include telehealth, price transparency, quality monitoring, small-business insurance pools, cross-state insurance buying, and public-option or Medicare-for-All ideas.

Countries pay for care in four main ways, shown in the table. The key question is who pays and who owns the hospitals.

rows: Government, for all medically necessary care
Required employer and employee contributions to funds
Employers and individuals, plus public programs for some groups

check.q: A nurse from Canada says, "The government paid for my care, but my doctor ran a private practice." Which system is this?
check.a: Socialized insurance. The government pays, but delivery is private. In socialized medicine, the state also owns facilities and employs physicians.

sections.heading: Who pays for care?
sections.keyIdea: Every bill is paid by public insurance, private insurance, out-of-pocket money, or a mix.
sections.body:
Public insurance is government-funded for people who meet eligibility rules. Examples are Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP (the Children's Health Insurance Program). Private insurance comes from companies, through an employer or bought by the client. An employer plan is still private, not public. Out-of-pocket money is what the client pays personally.

The nurse does not decide coverage. But payer source shapes the plan. It affects which rehab will accept the client, which drugs are covered, and how many home visits are approved. So ask about cost barriers early. Do not assume the client can follow the plan.

rows: Know eligibility basics to teach and refer
Blue Cross Blue Shield, Kaiser Permanente, Aetna
Networks, prior approval, and covered drug lists shape the plan
Ask about cost barriers; refer to social work

check.q: A client has an employer-sponsored plan from a private company. Is this public insurance?
check.a: No. Employer sponsorship does not make a plan public. Public insurance is government-funded, such as Medicare or Medicaid.

sections.heading: Medicare vs. Medicaid: what's the difference?
sections.keyIdea: Medicare is mainly about age or disability; Medicaid is about income and need, and covers long-term nursing-home care.
sections.body:
These two have similar names but different logic. Medicare is federal. It is based on age 65 and older, or certain disabilities and conditions. Income does not decide eligibility. Medicaid is joint federal–state and based mainly on income and need. Rules vary by state. A person can qualify for both.

A common trap is long-term care. Medicare covers short-term skilled nursing or rehab after a qualifying hospital stay, hospice, and home health when criteria are met. It does not pay for long-term custodial care, meaning help with bathing and dressing in a nursing home indefinitely. Medicaid is the major public payer for that care, for those who qualify.

rows: Age 65+, certain disabilities, end-stage renal disease (ESRD), ALS
Low income and other state criteria
Part A hospital, B outpatient, C Advantage, D drugs
Benefits set by each state within federal rules
CARE for those who are aging
AID for those with financial need

check.q: A 70-year-old says, "I can't get Medicare because I have savings." What should the nurse clarify?
check.a: Medicare is based on age or qualifying disability, not income. Savings affect Medicaid eligibility, not Medicare.

sections.heading: What do premium, deductible, and coinsurance mean?
sections.keyIdea: The premium keeps coverage, the deductible comes first, a co-pay is fixed dollars, and coinsurance is a percentage.
sections.body:
Clients are often surprised by bills because these words sound alike. Walking a client through them is teaching and advocacy. It also keeps clients from skipping care because they misunderstand what they owe.

An out-of-network penalty means higher cost for care outside the network or without meeting the rules. Examples are no referral in an HMO or no prior approval. A PPO client may see an out-of-network specialist without a referral but will likely pay more.

rows: PPO pays less for an out-of-network specialist

sections.example: A client has a $1,000 deductible, none met yet, and 20% coinsurance. A covered procedure costs $3,000. The client pays the first $1,000. Of the remaining $2,000, the client pays 20%, or $400. The total is $1,400, and the plan pays $1,600. A later $30 co-pay visit is owed on top of that.

check.q: A client says, "I pay my premium every month, so my MRI should be free." The $1,500 deductible is not met. What is accurate?
check.a: The premium keeps coverage active, but the plan usually starts paying only after the yearly deductible is met.

sections.heading: How do DRGs and prospective payment work?
sections.keyIdea: The hospital gets a fixed payment set in advance, so preventing complications and readmissions protects both clients and budgets.
sections.body:
Under a prospective payment system (PPS), Medicare and many payers set the payment in advance. It is based on the client's DRG. The payment does not rise if the client stays longer. If care costs less, the hospital keeps the difference. If it costs more, the hospital absorbs the loss.

This creates a good incentive: prevent complications and discharge on time. It also creates a risk: pressure for early discharge, which can raise readmissions.

Payers responded. Medicare does not pay extra for certain preventable hospital-acquired conditions. Examples are stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries, falls with injury, catheter urinary infections (CAUTI), and central line bloodstream infections (CLABSI). Medicare also penalizes hospitals with too many 30-day readmissions for selected conditions. The system now rewards what good nursing does.
sections.analogy: PPS is like a fixed-price catering deal. The caterer gets a set price per guest. A smart caterer avoids waste. A careless one runs out, and the guests come back angry.
sections.example: A client with a hip repair gets a stage 3 pressure injury because turning was missed. The stay grows by 6 days. The hospital gets about the same payment, so it absorbs the cost, and the client suffers. Turning every 2 hours, a skin check each shift, and nutrition support would have cost far less.

check.q: A client admitted for pneumonia gets a CAUTI that adds 3 days. Who bears most of the cost?
check.a: The hospital, because payment was set in advance and Medicare does not pay extra for this condition. Prevention is both safe and cost-effective care.

sections.heading: What can the bedside nurse do?
sections.keyIdea: The best ways to save money are safety actions; shortcuts that risk harm only move the cost into complications.
sections.body:
Nurses affect a big share of hospital costs through hourly care. The highest-value actions prevent costly harm and repeats. Knowing what not to do matters just as much. Reusing single-use items, skipping reassessments, or delegating RN work to save salary shifts cost into harm and readmission.

When a client cannot afford care, assess the barrier. Tell the provider, and refer to social work or case management. If a payer denies needed equipment, work with the case manager and provider to document need and appeal. Never tell a client to skip or space out a medication.
bullets: Prevent: falls, pressure injuries, CAUTI, CLABSI, blood clots (VTE), and aspiration.
Avoid repeats: check for labs already drawn; cluster care and lab draws.
Prepare for discharge: teach-back, an affordability check, follow-up within 7 days, home health or telehealth.
Advocate: social work, case management, and a lower-cost equal drug discussed with the provider.
Never: reuse single-use devices, skip assessments, delegate outside scope, or use a product that is wrong for the client.
sections.example: During discharge, a client with COPD says the new inhaler costs $350 a month. The nurse does not suggest skipping doses. The nurse asks about coverage, tells the provider so a covered option can be considered, and refers to social work before discharge.

check.q: A coworker suggests reusing a single-use suction catheter all shift to save money. What should the nurse say?
check.a: Decline. Reuse raises infection risk and breaks the standard of care. Suggest real savings instead, like checking for duplicate labs or clustering care.

sections.heading: Common traps: look-alikes to tell apart
sections.keyIdea: Many cost terms are near-twins; one clue in the stem usually separates them.
sections.body: Use the clue to sort these near-twins.

rows: Age 65+ or disability vs. low income and long-term custodial care
"$25 per visit" vs. "20% of the bill"
Keeps coverage active vs. paid before the plan pays
State pays and owns (UK) vs. state pays, providers private (Canada)
Law requires contributions (Germany) vs. mostly optional (U.S.)
The diagnosis category vs. the payment method that uses it
Best outcome for resources vs. cheapest option that may cause harm

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: When cost is the problem, assess, communicate with the prescriber, and refer; never reduce therapy on your own.
sections.body: Expect these patterns:
bullets: Teaching: coverage terms or Medicare vs. Medicaid, often as "which statement needs more teaching?"
Cost barrier: assess, involve the provider, and refer.
Cost vs. safety: reject the unsafe shortcut and offer a real efficiency.
Payment incentives: why preventing complications and readmissions matters under PPS.
steps: Read the stem: A client with heart failure says, "I can't afford all these pills, so I'll take the water pill every other day." Best response? (A) "That's fine if you weigh yourself." (B) "Let's look at what each medicine costs you. I'll tell your provider and ask the social worker about help." (C) "You must take every pill or you'll be readmitted." (D) "Ask your pharmacist which pills you can stop."
What is it really asking? How to handle a cost barrier causing unsafe nonadherence.
Key cues: skipping a diuretic risks fluid overload and readmission. The client named a cost problem.
Why the others are wrong: (A) approves an unsafe change. (C) threatens and solves nothing. (D) suggests stopping drugs without the prescriber.
The answer is (B). It assesses, informs the prescriber, and finds resources.
Reusable strategy: assess, communicate, refer. Never reduce therapy without the prescriber.

sections.heading: Worked case: the budget meeting
sections.keyIdea: Complications and readmissions drive cost more than RN salaries, so target prevention, not staffing cuts.
sections.body: You are charge nurse on a 24-bed unit. Length of stay is above the DRG benchmark. Last quarter there were 4 CAUTIs and 3 falls with injury. Heart failure readmissions are 24%. A manager proposes replacing two RNs with UAP and buying a cheaper skin barrier. You are asked for a plan.
steps: Notice cues: CAUTIs and falls are preventable and not paid extra. Readmissions bring penalties. Cutting RNs lowers RN hours on a unit with acuity problems.
Analyze: the biggest costs are complications and readmissions. RN staffing and education are linked to lower death rates and fewer adverse events.
Plan: a nurse-driven catheter removal protocol; a stronger fall bundle; a heart failure discharge bundle with teach-back, affordability checks, follow-up within 7 days, and telehealth weights.
Supplies: a cheaper barrier is fine only if it works as well and is not wrong for the client.
Act: present the plan through the unit practice council (shared governance).
Evaluate: track infections, falls, length of stay, readmissions, supply costs, and satisfaction monthly.

check.q: The manager asks, "Why not replace RNs with UAP? It saves salary." What is the best reply?
check.a: RN staffing and education are linked to illness, death, and cost. Fewer RN hours mean more missed assessments and complications. Match skill mix to acuity, and target the complications driving cost.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: Budget pressure never changes North Carolina's rules on who may do what.
sections.body: In North Carolina, cost pressure does not change the law:
bullets: The NC Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and NCBON rules (21 NCAC 36 .0224 for RNs, .0225 for LPNs) keep assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment with the RN.

Nurse Aide I (registry kept by NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation) and Nurse Aide II (registry kept by NCBON; also on the NA I registry) may do only tasks on their approved lists, when the RN decides it fits the client.
Replacing licensed staff with aides cannot expand those lists.
A disabled adult who seems neglected or financially exploited: under G.S. 108A-102, anyone with reasonable cause must report to the county DSS director. Good-faith reporters are immune.

End-of-life talks center on the client's wishes, not cost. NC tools: Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3), Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (G.S. 90-321), and the MOST form.

sections.body: Source: Module 39 study guide, Exemplar 39.B, p. 2630: public and private insurance, socialized medicine and insurance, the U.S. cost crisis, payment and cost-sharing terms, and international views. The source notes DRGs, PPS, mandatory and voluntary insurance continue on pp. 2631–2632. DRGs also appear on p. 2627.
bullets: The Commonwealth Fund comparisons are with high-income peer countries, not all countries.
The source's two definitions of socialized insurance are combined: government pays, providers largely private (Canada).
Added mandatory and voluntary insurance with standard examples, plus a PPS definition, to complete the framework.
Added coinsurance, premium, Medicare parts, Medicaid long-term care, and CMS hospital-acquired condition and readmission policies.
"Client" replaces the source's "patient."

mnemonics.name: Co-pay is Constant; coinsurance is perCentage
mnemonics.text: Co-pay = fixed dollars per service. Coinsurance = a percent after the deductible.

mnemonics.name: Pay-Own grid
mnemonics.text: Socialized medicine: government Pays and Owns. Socialized insurance: government Pays, private Owns. Mandatory: law Makes you pay in. Voluntary: you Volunteer to buy (U.S.).

pearls: The most cost-effective nursing actions are safety actions.
Under PPS, complications and extra days are mostly unpaid costs.
Medicare is not income-based; Medicaid is.
Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial nursing-home care.
Telehealth saves cost and improves access for rural and chronically ill clients.
redFlags: A client plans to skip, split, or space out a key medication because of cost.
A cost-saving idea that reuses single-use devices, skips reassessment, or delegates RN work.
Early discharge without teach-back, follow-up, or a way to get medications.
A client who avoids care because of a misunderstood bill.

checks.q: A client has met the deductible and has 20% coinsurance. A covered procedure costs $2,000. What will the client owe?
A nurse suggests leaving urinary catheters in until discharge to save time. Why is this not cost-effective?
checks.a: It raises CAUTI risk. CAUTI harms clients, lengthens stays, and is not paid extra by Medicare. Insert catheters only when needed and remove them as soon as they are no longer indicated.

checks.q: An uninsured client with cellulitis says, "I probably won't fill the antibiotic." What should the nurse do first?
checks.a: Explore the cost concern and involve the provider and social work.

checks.q: A rural client with heart failure misses visits because the clinic is 80 miles away. What helps cost and access?
checks.a: Telehealth visits with daily remote weight monitoring.

checks.q: A client with a spinal cord injury has a Medicaid power wheelchair denied and says, "I'll just stay in bed." What shows advocacy?
checks.a: Work with the case manager and provider to document need and appeal.
